course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

topic.title: Sine and Cosine Function Graphs
topic.summary: The sine and cosine functions as the vertical and horizontal displacements of a point moving around the unit circle, their domains, their outputs between −1 and 1, and how to sketch their graphs.

lesson.title: Sine and Cosine Function Graphs
lesson.summary: The sine and cosine functions as the vertical and horizontal displacements of a point moving around the unit circle, their domains, their outputs between −1 and 1, and how to sketch their graphs.
learningGoals: 3.4.A Construct representations of the sine and cosine functions using the unit circle.
lesson.bigIdea: As an angle θ grows, the point P where its terminal ray meets the unit circle travels around and around. Plotting P's y-coordinate against θ gives the graph of sine; plotting its x-coordinate gives the graph of cosine.
lesson.context: Topics 3.2 and 3.3 found sine and cosine one angle at a time. This topic treats them as functions of θ and turns the unit circle into the two graphs used for the rest of the unit.

sections.title: 3.4.A · The sine function gives the vertical displacement of P from the x-axis.
sections.conceptTitle: The sine function and its graph

blocks.text: Given an angle of measure θ in standard position and a unit circle centered at the origin, there is a point, P, where the terminal ray intersects the circle. The sine function, f(θ) = sin θ, gives the y-coordinate, or vertical displacement from the x-axis, of point P. The domain of the sine function is all real numbers.

As the input values, or angle measures, of the sine function increase, the output values oscillate between −1 and 1, taking every value in between and tracking the vertical displacement of points on the unit circle from the x-axis.

blocks.caption: y = sin θ. Move the slider to send P around the unit circle; the marked point shows (a, sin a).
blocks.alt: A wave that starts at the origin, rises to 1 at π/2, returns to 0 at π, falls to −1 at 3π/2, and returns to 0 at 2π. The same shape repeats for negative angles. A marked point sits on the curve at the slider's angle.

blocks.caption: Where P is on the unit circle and the value of sin θ

sections.takeaway: sin θ is P's height above or below the x-axis; it never leaves −1 ≤ y ≤ 1.

sections.title: 3.4.A · The cosine function gives the horizontal displacement of P from the y-axis.
sections.conceptTitle: The cosine function and its graph

blocks.text: Given an angle of measure θ in standard position and a unit circle centered at the origin, there is a point, P, where the terminal ray intersects the circle. The cosine function, f(θ) = cos θ, gives the x-coordinate, or horizontal displacement from the y-axis, of point P. The domain of the cosine function is all real numbers.

As the input values, or angle measures, of the cosine function increase, the output values oscillate between −1 and 1, taking every value in between and tracking the horizontal displacement of points on the unit circle from the y-axis.

blocks.caption: y = cos θ (solid) and y = sin θ (dashed)
blocks.alt: Two waves. The solid cosine wave starts at 1 when θ = 0, falls to 0 at π/2, to −1 at π, back to 0 at 3π/2, and 1 at 2π. The dashed sine wave has the same shape, a quarter turn later.

blocks.text: Example: as θ increases from π to 3π/2, P moves from (−1, 0) to (0, −1). Its x-coordinate goes from −1 to 0, so cos θ increases, while its y-coordinate goes from 0 to −1, so sin θ decreases.

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: On 0 < θ < π/2, cos θ is decreasing because P moves toward the y-axis, so its horizontal displacement from the y-axis shrinks from 1 to 0.

sections.takeaway: cos θ is P's horizontal position; sine and cosine have the same shape, a quarter turn apart.

connections.title: Exact values become points
connections.body: The exact values from Topic 3.3 give points on these graphs. For example, (π/6, 1/2) is on the graph of y = sin θ and (π/6, √3/2) is on the graph of y = cos θ.
connections.transferQuestion: Name the point on the graph of y = cos θ with θ = 2π/3.

connections.title: Sinusoidal functions
connections.body: Topic 3.5 calls sine and cosine sinusoidal functions and names their period, frequency, amplitude, and midline.
connections.transferQuestion: From the graph, after how long an interval of θ does y = sin θ start to repeat?

glossary.definition: The period of the function is the smallest positive value k such that f(x + k) = f(x) for all x in the domain. Consequently, the behavior of a periodic function is completely determined by any interval of width k.
In the coordinate plane, an angle is in standard position when the vertex coincides with the origin and one ray coincides with the positive x-axis. The other ray is called the terminal ray.

In the coordinate plane, an angle is in standard position when the vertex coincides with the origin and one ray coincides with the positive x-axis. The other ray is called the terminal ray. Positive and negative angle measures indicate rotations from the positive x-axis in the counterclockwise and clockwise direction, respectively. Angles in standard position that share a terminal ray differ by an integer number of revolutions.
